column5: write the song, teach it, put it in mouths
column6: God commands Moses to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths. It is a particularly exact Mosaic pairing of written witness, recitation, memory, and a resistant audience.

column5: king writes a Torah copy in a book
column6: The king must write his own Torah copy from the priestly exemplar. This develops the commentary's concern with sheets as authoritative, transmissible written objects rather than an abstract antiquity.

column5: daily reading of the written Torah
column6: The king reads the written Torah all his life in order to fear God and obey. It supplies an older scriptural account of a page becoming enduring ethical formation.

column5: book in the mouth and day-night meditation
column6: Joshua's law-book must not leave his mouth but be meditated on and done. It closely joins the commentary's page, oral recitation, internal remembering, and conduct.

column5: prophetic words dictated onto a scroll
column6: Baruch writes on a scroll all the words Jeremiah has spoken from the prophet's mouth. It gives a precise Hebrew Bible instance of oral revelation becoming separate written pages.

column5: seek and read the book of YHWH
column6: Isaiah orders hearers to seek and read YHWH's book, whose announced creatures are not missing. It makes a preserved prior writing an available public check on a present claim.

column5: word accomplishes its purpose
column6: The word sent from God's mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose. It supplies a close biblical analogue to the commentary's ta'wil: a spoken word reaches the end it declares.

column5: the dead live and awake
column6: Isaiah calls the dead to live and those in dust to awake. It gives a direct Hebrew Bible answer to the commentary's concern for the first generations and their future gathering.

column5: bread and every word from God's mouth
column6: Manna teaches that life is not sustained by bread alone but by every word from God. This is a concrete predecessor to preferring a lasting divine word over immediate provision.

column5: heard word received as God's, not human
column6: Paul commends hearers for receiving the proclaimed word as God's rather than a human word. It directly addresses the commentary's anticipated charge that revelation is merely the speaker's own speech.

column5: message received through revelation, not human teaching
column6: Paul says he neither received nor learned his gospel from a human source but through revelation. This provides a Christian analogue to the commentary's contrast between ordinary textual learning and revealed recitation.

column5: prophecy not from human will
column6: Prophecy is said not to arise from human will, but from people speaking from God while carried by the Holy Spirit. It gives an explicit Christian response to the invention accusation developed around 87:18.

column5: Deuteronomy's word in mouth and heart reapplied
column6: Paul cites the Torah's word as near in mouth and heart and identifies it with the proclaimed word of faith. This is a direct Christian rereading of the oral-and-inward Torah motif beside the commentary's recited former pages.

column5: Scripture fulfilled in the hearers' hearing
column6: After reading Isaiah's scroll, Jesus says the Scripture is fulfilled today in the audience's hearing. It closely models the commentary's claim that an old written word becomes present through a current recitation.

column5: seen things temporary, unseen things eternal
column6: Paul explicitly contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal. It is a direct Christian formulation of the commentary's near-world versus enduring-future opposition.

column5: no lasting city here, city to come
column6: Hebrews denies that believers have a lasting city here and directs them toward the one to come. This gives a concrete social image to the commentary's preference for the abiding later life.

column5: cleansing ourselves in fear of God
column6: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and complete holiness in fear of God. The reflexive language and fear make it a close counterpart to the commentary's tazakka and yahsha.

column5: washing sins while calling the name
column6: Paul is told to wash away sins while calling on the Lord's name. It directly binds purification to name-invocation, two elements the commentary brings together around 87:14-15.

column5: enduring word identified with preached good news
column6: The Lord's word remains forever, and the letter identifies that enduring word with the good news preached to its hearers. It is a Christian reception of the commentary's old-word-to-present-voice claim.

column5: one reads, others hear, all keep written prophecy
column6: Revelation blesses the reader, the hearers, and those who keep a written prophecy. The verse gives a compact Christian scene in which a text, voiced reading, and ethical response remain inseparable.

column5: this world as vestibule before the world to come
column6: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the World to Come and urges preparation for entry. It provides a concise rabbinic analogue to the commentary's near life ordered toward a lasting later reality.

column5: a share in the world to come
column6: The Mishnah opens its judgment discussion by assigning Israel a share in the World to Come while naming exclusions. It supplies a Jewish communal and ethical frame for the commentary's decisive future outcome.

column5: World to Come beyond eating and drinking
column6: The Talmud portrays the World to Come as beyond eating and drinking, with the righteous enjoying the divine presence. It sharpens the commentary's contrast between immediate material life and enduring eschatological enjoyment.

column5: deeds with fruit now and principal in the world to come
column6: The Mishnah distinguishes the present fruit of certain deeds from their enduring principal in the World to Come. This is a precise Jewish counterpart to present action receiving a later, fuller outcome.

column5: testimony bound and teaching sealed
column6: Isaiah binds and seals testimony among disciples. It offers a counter-image to the commentary's open sheets: teaching is preserved, yet access is marked by a bounded circle of transmitters.

column5: visions from a prophet's own heart
column6: Jeremiah warns against prophets who speak visions from their own hearts rather than YHWH's mouth. It supplies the Hebrew Bible's own criterion for the human-invention charge that 87:18 rhetorically rejects.

column5: present repentance and future bliss compared
column6: Avot calls one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world greater than all the World to Come, then calls one hour of World-to-Come bliss greater than all worldly life. Its two-sided comparison complicates, yet productively parallels, the commentary's simple worldly-versus-lasting contrast.
